Cloudburst-induced floods disrupt life in Gilgit-Baltistan's Ghizer, Hunza. Karakoram Highway being cleared in Murtazaabad, Hunza.—Photo by the writer • Floods damage homes, farmland and orchards; roads blocked • Babusar Top gets season’s first snowfall as experts warn of changing weather patterns GILGIT: Cloudburst-induced flo­ods blocked the Karakoram Highway (KKH) and other roads, damaged farmland and properties and disrupted electricity supply in Ghizer district on Saturday. Flash floods triggered by heavy rain caused damage to houses and crops in several areas of Ghizer in the early hours. The floods wreaked havoc in Naubahar village, damaging Gush­gush Jamaat Khana. They also destroyed crops, fruit trees and agricultural land in the village. Floods in various areas blocked the road from Immit to Barjangle and damaged electricity transmission lines along the route. Residents were cut off from other areas following the blockade and demanded that the administration take emergency measures to reopen the affected road and provide immediate assistance to flood victims to compensate for their losses. Meanwhile, according to the Gilgit-Baltistan police spokesperson, the KKH was completely closed from Sost to Khunjerab Top due to landslides. He said relevant agencies were working to restore the highway. Tourists have been advised to avoid unnecessary travel in view of the situation. The tourism police said the section of the KKH between Murta­zaabad and Hassanabad village in Hunza had been reopened for traffic after being blocked by landslides. Panic among residents While intermittent rain, thunderstorms and lightning have continued across Gilgit-Baltistan since Aug 1, locals said they had never experienced such downpour. Wase­­em Baigal, a resident of Gilgit, told Dawn that thunderstorms and heavy rain caused panic among locals. He said he had never experienced such heavy rain and thunderstorms in his life. However, he added that the rain had not caused any damage in his area. Meanwhile, continuous rainfall has brought down temperatures across Gilgit-Baltistan. According to the Diamer district administration, Babusar Top received snowfall on Saturday morning. It was the first snowfall of the season, but vehicular traffic continued on Babusar Road. Changing weather patterns According to the GB Disaster Management Authority, the region experienced 120 floods triggered by cloudbursts and melting glaciers from June to August this year. The floods destroyed dozens of homes, farmland, orchards, trees, irrigation channels and roads, besides damaging electricity supply systems. Residents in several areas remained stranded for days. Experts said the region had und­e­rgone a shift in weather patterns, with frequent floods, cloudburst-induced floods, rapid glacier melting, glacial lake outburst floods, landslides and high temperatures. They said the fragile ecosystem of the region was under increasing threat from climate change, while residents living among more than 8,000 glaciers, 300 glacial lakes and mountains faced increasingly severe disasters. Ali Ahmed, a resident, said mid-August was traditionally considered the summer season, after which the weather started turning cold. “According to indigenous knowledge, ice started to freeze at high altitudes and the risk of flash floods was over. However, for the last many years, a weather shift has been experienced,” he added. Safdar Ali, another resident, said people in Gilgit-Baltistan were among the most vulnerable to the impacts of climate change. He said increasing climate-related impacts had created panic among local residents. Published in Dawn, September 6th, 2026

PM, president highlight Pakistan's growing role in regional security as nation observes Defence Day. Prime Minister Shehbaz Sharif and President Asif Zardari highlighted Pakistan’s growing role in regional security on Sunday as the nation observed on 61st Defence and Martyrs’ Day. The day began with thirty-one gun salute in Islamabad and twenty-one gun salute at provincial capitals, state broadcaster Radio Pakistan reported. A change of guards was also held at the Quaid’s mausoleum in Karachi. The Defence Day is observed every year on September 6 to commemorate the legacy of the 1965 war , which began after India launched an attack across the international border. The war ended with a ceasefire on September 22, and peace between the two countries was negotiated under Soviet auspices in Tashkent on January 10, 1966. During this war, 1617 square miles of territory was occupied by Pakistan as compared to 446 square miles of Pakistan’s open and undefended territory occupied by India. The Pakistan Army had captured 20 Indian officers, 19 junior Indian commissioned officers and 569 other ranks. PM’s message PM Shehbaz paid tribute to the martyrs and veterans of armed forces and their families, on behalf of the entire nation, in his Defence Day message issued by his office. “September 6 is a glorious chapter in our national history, reminding us of the unparalleled resolve, unity and sacrifices demonstrated by our armed forces and the nation in defence of our beloved homeland. “This day provides us with an opportunity to pay tribute to the martyrs and veterans who made immense sacrifices to safeguard Pakistan’s security, sovereignty and independence. Despite the enemy’s undeclared aggression and numerical superiority on September 6 1965, the professionalism and operational preparedness of Pakistan’s armed forces inflicted a humiliating and resounding defeat upon it on all fronts,” he recalled. The prime minister added, “History bears witness that during the 1965 war, our armed forces displayed exceptional professionalism and courage, while the Pakistani nation demonstrated remarkable unity, resilience and steadfastness. Together they created a proud and enduring legacy in our national history.” The prime minister also commended the armed forces’ response to India during last-year four-day military conflict, Marka-i-Haq . “In line with the glorious tradition of valiance, our armed forces, under the excellent professional strategy of Chief of Defence Forces and Chief of Army Staff Field Marshal Syed Asim Munir, Air Chief Marshal Zaheer Ahmad Babar Sidhu and Naval Chief Admiral Naveed Ashraf, delivered a response to our age-old adversary that will be remembered for generations. “The entire nation is proud of our brave Pakistan Army, Pakistan Air Force and Pakistan Navy,” he said. Referring to Bunyanum Marsoos —Pakistan’s military operation in response to India’s attack in the episode — the premier said its success added another “glorious chapter to our military history”. “Our armed forces have once again demonstrated that the spirit and fervour of September 6 remain as strong as ever.” He added that the challenges confronting Pakistan today demanded greater national unity and solidarity. “Our traditional adversary, along with Fitna-al-Khawarij and Fitna-al-Hindustan, continues to pursue its nefarious designs against Pakistan, but these hostile forces are facing successive and decisive defeats. The sinister designs of hostile forces seeking to destabilise Pakistan through hybrid warfare shall be resolutely defeated,” he said. The state uses the term Fitna-al-Khawarij for the banned Tehreek-i-Taliban Pakistan (TTP) and has designated Balochistan-based groups as Fitna-al-Hindustan to highlight India’s alleged role in terrorism and destabilisation across Pakistan. Beyond security challenges, PM Shehbaz said one of the country’s “foremost challenge is to eradicate ignorance, poverty and backwardness and to transform Pakistan in accordance with the vision of Quaid-o-Azam Mohammad Ali Jinnah and Allama Muhammad Iqbal”. “Our true strength lies not only in our defence capabilities but also in a united, peaceful, stable and economically strong nation,” he said, adding that the government would continue to take resolute measures to strengthen Pakistan’s security, sovereignty and defence, while simultaneously advancing economic development, political stability and public welfare. And beyond its frontiers, Pakistan would continue to play an “active and constructive” role in promoting peace and stability at both regional and global levels, he added. As a responsible state, Pakistan had emerged as a net security stabiliser, contributing to collective security, peace and stability beyond its borders, he said, adding that the Makkah Defence Alliance was a manifestation of Pakistan’s growing role in regional security and reflected its commitment to collective defence, mutual security and enduring partnerships with brotherly countries. “Pakistan will continue to fulfil its responsibilities as a dependable partner for peace and security while pursuing cooperation and dialogue as the preferred means of addressing regional challenges,” he said. He then called on the international community to recognise that lasting and genuine peace in South Asia could not be achieved without resolution of the Kashmir issue as per United Nations Security Council resolutions and the aspirations of the people of Kashmir. “Quaid-i-Azam described Kashmir as Pakistan’s jugular vein. India’s reprehensible conduct and continued intransigence on the Kashmir dispute remain major impediments to lasting peace, development and prosperity in the region,” he said. Coming back to September 6, he added, “On this historic day, let us renew our commitment to making Quaid-i-Azam Mohammad Ali Jinnah’s principles of faith, unity and discipline an integral part of our national life. Let us work together to build a strong, prosperous and developed Pakistan. “We must always remember that a strong defence provides the foundation for sustainable peace and development. The armed forces of Pakistan remain the guarantors of our national security, and the entire nation stands shoulder to shoulder with its brave defenders,” he said. President’s message President Zardari began his message by stating that September 6 held a “memorable place in our national history, reminding us of the great sacrifices made to safeguard our freedom, sovereignty and national security”. “Defence and Martyrs’ Day provides us with an opportunity to pay tribute to the immortal sacrifices of the brave sons of the nation who, in 1965, demonstrated unparalleled resolve, courage and devotion in defence of our beloved homeland, defeating the enemy’s nefarious designs on every front. “I, on behalf of the entire nation, salute the martyrs and veterans of Pakistan’s armed forces and their families. Through their blood and sacrifice, our martyrs wrote timeless stories of courage and patriotism in the annals of our national history. Their sacrifices will forever remain a guiding light for generations to come,” he said. The president said the unity and spirit of faith demonstrated by the armed forces and the Pakistani nation on September 6, 1965 remained a manifestation of the nation’s collective strength. “This day reminds us that when a nation stands united in defence of its freedom, sovereignty and homeland, no power can defeat its resolve,” he added. He, too, recalled Marka-i-Haq, saying that the “spirit of September 6 was once again reflected in the resounding success of Operation Bunyanum Marsoos”. “Victory in Marka-i-Haq represents a continuation of the spirit of patriotism and freedom embodied by September 6. Marka-i-Haq has added another glorious chapter to our national history. This extraordinary success is a testament to the professionalism, courage and bravery of our armed forces and reflects the exemplary longstanding bond between the armed forces and the people of Pakistan,” he said. He too mentioned Pakistan’s role in regional security, and said that as a peaceful and responsible state, the country remained firmly committed to promoting peace, dialogue and mutual respect in the region and across the world. “Pakistan has increasingly emerged as a net regional security provider, contributing to peace, stability and collective security beyond its frontiers. The Makkah Joint Defence Agreement is a manifestation of Pakistan’s commitment to regional security and its growing role as a responsible and dependable partner for regional peace and stability,” he said. At the same time, he continued, there could be no compromise on Pakistan’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and national security. “The international community must recognise that lasting peace in South Asia cannot be achieved without resolution of the Kashmir issue as per United Nations Security Council resolutions and the aspirations of the people of Kashmir,” the president said. He further called on India to “desist from promoting terrorism in Pakistan through its proxies”. “United Nations reports testify that Fitna-al-Khawarij and Fitna-al-Hindustan have received foreign patronage and the nexus between India and the Taliban regime is no longer a secret,” he noted. The president added that in every conventional and unconventional war, Pakistan’s armed forces had demonstrated their vigilance, preparedness and unwavering commitment to defending the country. “The entire nation continues to stand shoulder to shoulder with its brave armed forces,” he said. He added, “We must also remember that, alongside a strong defence, economic stability, political tolerance, national unity, education and development constitute the foundations of Pakistan’s strength. Together, we must play our part in building a bright, secure and developed Pakistan for our youth and future generations.” The president concluded his message, saying: “Today, as we pay tribute to the great sacrifices of our martyrs, we renew our resolve to defend Pakistan’s freedom, sovereignty and security at all costs. We also reaffirm our commitment to working together to transform Pakistan, in accordance with the vision of Quaid-i-Azam Mohammad Ali Jinnah, into a strong, democratic, prosperous and developed state.” ‘Pakistan seeks peace in region’ Country’s top miliatry brass also commemorated the war’s legacy on the day in a message released by the military’s media affairs wing. The Inter-Services Public Relations (ISPR) statement said CDF Munir, Admiral Ashraf, Air Chief Marshal Sidhu National Strategic Command Commander General Syed Aamer Raza and the armed forces “pay profound tribute to the shuhada (martyrs) of Pakistan and extend their deepest respect and gratitude to the ghazis (fighters) and the families of our martyrs on the occasion of the 61st Defence and Martyrs’ Day”. “September 6 remains an enduring symbol of national unity, courage and resolve, reminding us how the Pakistani nation stood as one in defence of the motherland during the war of 1965,” the statement said. It added that martyrs of Pakistan “embody the highest ideals of honour, duty and sacrifice”. “Across the battlefields, skies and seas, generations of Pakistan’s defenders have stood sentinels and made the ultimate sacrifice in service to the nation. Their immortal legacy continues to inspire future generations, while the families of our shuhada remain enduring symbols of fortitude and resilience. “We also salute our ghazis , who continue to guard the nation’s frontiers with valour, steadfastness and distinguished service,” the statement said. The armed forces remained fully prepared to defend the country’s sovereignty, territorial integrity and national interests, it said, adding that Pakistan sought peace, stability and prosperity in the region and remained committed to responsible conduct and peaceful coexistence. “This commitment, however, must never be mistaken for weakness. Any aggression against Pakistan will be met with a swift and decisive response.” The armed forces renewed their “solemn pledge of unwavering devotion to Pakistan and its people”. “The supreme sacrifices of our shuhada , the spirit of our ghazis and the fortitude of their families will forever remain a source of national strength and pride. Standing united with the nation, the armed forces will continue to discharge their sacred responsibilities with honour, professionalism and unflinching resolve,” the statement said. Separately, Air Vice Marshal Hasan Faisal addressed the change of guards ceremony at the Quaid’s mausoleum, saying that September 6 reminded the nation of when the armed forces defeated “the enemy’s nefarious ambitions”. “The founder of Pakistan gave us the motto of unity, faith and sacrifice,” he said. “Today we remember, as watchmen of the Quaid’s mausoleum, that we will always stand in defence of the motherland,” he added. Referring to both the wars of 1965 and 1971 between Pakistan and India as well as last year’s Marka-i-Haq conflict, he said that the air force had always upheld the hopes of the public. “Whether foreign conspiracies or combating natural disasters, […] PAF has always kept the security of the country as its primary goal,” he said. He noted that in last year’s conflict, the national political leadership provided guidance with an “unrelenting desire and wisdom” that allowed India’s defeat at the hands of Pakistan. “Today, in keeping with the occasion, I assure you all that the defence of Pakistan’s aerial borders is in the strong hands of PAF,” he said. He highlighted the leadership of Air Chief Marshal Zaheer Ahmed Babar Siddhu that he said made PAF “a max-generation air force, at the top of the world in niche technologies, advanced weapons systems, space, cyber, AI and IT”.

Climate test. THE world is edging into climate territory governments have spent years trying to avoid. A new UN Environment Programme report warns that the Paris Agreement’s 1.5°C warming threshold is likely to be breached within the next few years. That does not mean climate action has failed or that the target no longer matters. UNEP argues that humanity must keep any “overshoot” as low and brief as possible, as every fraction of warming raises the risk of extreme weather, ecosystem loss and irreversible tipping points. Adding to the concern, the World Meteorological Organisation says the El Niño strengthening in the Pacific could be the strongest in four decades, intensifying heat, drought and floods worldwide. For Pakistan, the fallout could include water stress, food insecurity and greater strain on urban infrastructure and services. The Nepal-China floods have shown how quickly climate hazards can devastate lives. As warming intensifies, Pakistan will increasingly have to contend with several climate stresses at once, often in places least equipped to cope. That demands a rethink of how the country plans for development. Pakistan must plan for a climate changing faster than its institutions. Adaptation cannot remain confined to emergency response after floods, heatwaves or droughts. Development policy itself must change. New housing, roads, power systems and urban drainage should be built for harsher weather. Water policy must account for uncertain river flows and rainfall. Agriculture needs crops and irrigation methods better suited to greater heat and water stress, along with support to help farmers adapt. Cities require heat-action plans, shaded public spaces and stronger protection for outdoor workers. A World Bank assessment covering Pakistan and the wider MENAAP region found that prolonged extreme heat is depressing sales, labour productivity and wages, showing that climate damage is also an economic competitiveness problem. None of this absolves the major emitters. UNEP identifies finance, equity and global cooperation as essential to navigating a dangerous climate future, while stressing that countries with greater responsibility for global warming must act fastest. Pakistan should press that case. But it must also spend development resources intelligently. The age of treating climate disasters as one-off emergencies has ended and it must plan for a harsher reality. Published in Dawn, September 6th, 2026

Top US military officials face lie detectors in leak hunt. WASHINGTON: The Pentagon has launched a lie-detector dragnet to comb through high-ranking military officials and identify who leaked information about US munitions stockpiles, according to US press reports. In July, reports emerged that the Un­­­i­­ted States was rationing munitions — its missile interceptors, in pa­­­­­r­­ticular — over supply concerns after several months of fighting Iran. Administration officials vehemently denied those reports, with President Donald Trump saying “we have a lot of ammunition, different types,” while acknowledging that “for some of the more sophisticated stuff, we’d certainly like to have more.” Late on Friday, The New York Times reported that some 50 members of the military’s Joint Staff — the Pentagon’s planning and advisory staff — were being required to take polygraph tests as part of an investigation into how classified stockpile information made its way into journalists’ hands. The polygraph tests aim to find out who leaked information about munition depletion to the media CBS News later also reported the wide-scale use of lie detectors, while adding that the chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, General Dan Caine, had not been tested. Both outlets cited unnamed officials. Asked about the reports, the Pentagon’s chief spokesman, Sean Parnell, refused to comment on “internal personnel or investigative matters,” but said that it “takes all leaks of classified national security information extremely seriously and investigates accordingly.” “Securing classified information is critical to ensuring the security of the United States and of our troops deployed around the world,” Parnell added. Both the Times and CBS noted the scale of the polygraph testing. Lie-detection testing is routine during background screenings and security clearance renewals for government staff with access to the most sensitive state secrets. But the wide-scale deployment of the detectors as part of a leak investigation was rare, if unprecedented, the outlets reported, citing analysts and unnamed officials. Ammunition stockpiles leaks The Pentagon launched an unprecedented investigation subjecting roughly 50 senior military officers and civilian employees to polygraph tests following media leaks regarding depleted US ammunition stockpiles from military conflict with Iran. Searching for past glory. THE collective memory of Muslim societies, particularly in the West and South Asia, is based on the persistent idea that since the collapse of the Ottoman Empire they have been in need of a joint response to challenges ranging from politics to defence. Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman of Saudi Arabia may be seen as something of a pioneer on this front with the creation of the Islamic Military Alliance to Fight Terrorism in 2015, which was partly the basis for the recently concluded Makkah Joint Defence Agreement . However, Pakistan has always championed such ambitions. The roots go much further back, with the Baghdad Pact representing an important milestone in that journey. The concept of a collective Muslim response has been conceived and framed in different ways, from the idea of the ummah to its more structured institutional expression within the Organisation of Islamic Cooperation. Its character has continued to evolve as changing political objectives have redirected the ideological orientation of Muslim states. In Pakistan’s case, however, this idea has shaped not only the country’s ideology but also its internal politics and models of state structure. There is little doubt that Pakistan’s growing role in the Gulf, beginning with Trump’s Gaza peace plan , followed by the Islamabad MoU and now the Makkah accord, has boosted the country’s confidence. However, when its leadership looks inward at the political and economic conditions, the contrast undermines some of the confidence gained from its successes in an evolving geopolitical environment. This disparity frustrates the power elite, that wants to address internal problems immediately and sustain the country’s momentum in the external arena. To achieve internal stability and order comparable to that in Saudi Arabia and Turkiye, Pakistan’s other regional partners, the power elite here appears prepared to take several political risks. These could include major administrative engineering, such as the creation of new provinces , a step that would come at considerable political cost. Pakistan is deepening its West Asian ties to bolster its defence power and strategic weight. This argument is not intended to evaluate the costs and benefits of creating new provinces. Rather, it seeks to trace the trigger that makes the power elite nervous when its external successes do not correspond with domestic political realities and the state of the economy. There can be several interpretations of this contradiction, ranging from the political economy to the changing geopolitical order. Yet an important dimension is often missing from the debate: the triangle of ideology, statecraft and geography. Pakistan and Turkiye share a geographical anxiety: their military power and ambitions do not fully correspond with the territories they control, while their opportunities for geographical expansion are extremely limited. This creates a middle-power anxiety about sustaining and enhancing their military and defence capabilities. Both countries are responding to this challenge in their own ways. Turkiye is pursuing regional groupings, alliances and transnational Turkic partnerships. Pakistan, meanwhile, appears to be abandoning its old strategy of ‘strategic depth’ or the attempt to expand its influence to neighbouring territories to overcome its geographical anxieties. Instead, it is engaging more deeply in West Asia to strengthen its defence capabilities and strategic weight. The purpose is obvious: Pakistan faces a much larger geographical and military power in India. Saudi Arabia faces a different middle-power dilemma. Its primary concerns are sustaining economic stability and protecting itself from regional forces that it perceives as ideologically hostile or hegemonically ambitious, principally Iran and Israel. Saudi Arabia has learned to coexist with Israel, but Israel’s hegemonic ambitions continue to generate anxiety about the future regional order. Riyadh is also concerned about hostile forces near its borders, particularly in Yemen, where Iran has effectively projected its influence. Pakistan is now going a step further by undergoing a state-centric ideological recalibration. This transformation does not yet match Saudi-style social liberalisation or the secular-nationalist transformation associated with Nasser’s Egypt. Pakistan is still struggling to find a clear direction. Its emerging model appears to combine Mohammed bin Salman’s state-controlled “moderate Islam”, the mutually reinforcing nationalism, military authority and state-regulated religious discourse of Abdel Fattah el-Sisi’s Egypt, and Turkiye’s religious-conservative identity, nationalism and defence-industrial ambition. Briefly, the power elite wants religion to remain under state authority. It seeks a transition from transnational Islamic solidarity to the national interest; the creation of a modern, technologically capable Muslim state; religious scholars who support national cohesion rather than challenge statecraft or the ambitions of the ruling elite; and centralised control over security and foreign policy. However, the power elite also believes that the existing political order, governance model and constitutional arrangements obstruct the achievement of lasting stability. Interestingly, the Afghan Taliban, once close allies of Pakistan’s establishment, have taught it an important lesson: Islamist allies may possess their own nationalism, interests and territorial ambitions, which may not correspond with the vision of another country’s power elite. Middle powers with complicated neighbourhoods and significant defence capabilities often have additional strategic thoughts. They imagine renewed glory through alliances with friendly states possessing compatible capabilities and ambition. Major powers frequently exploit this tendency by encouraging middle powers to form alliances. Washington is encouraging the emerging defence architecture that has taken shape through the Makkah accord. China and Iran, meanwhile, are waiting for the US to reduce its regional footprint before revealing or advancing their own designs. The US and UK exploited this middle-power tendency several times during the Cold War. The Baghdad Pact was the most developed form of such an alliance. Established in the mid-1950s, it brought together Turkiye, Pakistan, Iraq, Iran and the UK. However, the project eventually collapsed due to internal upheavals in Iraq and Iran, and Turkiye also experienced domestic political instability. At that time, Pakistan was considered the alliance’s most stable regional partner, with politics largely under control and an economy that appeared to be flourishing. Pakistan’s power elite still dreams of returning to those days of perceived glory and reclaiming the country’s position among the leading middle powers of the Muslim world. The writer is a security analyst. Published in Dawn, September 6th, 2026

Meltdown in PCB. ANYONE who has even casually followed Pakistan cricket over the years will know that our cricket board’s response to losing the current Test series in England is a hysterical overreaction. After consecutive defeats at Headingley and Lord’s sealed the fate of the three-match rubber, the Pakistan Cricket Board sacked the head coach and fast-bowling coach, ordered seven players from the squad to pack their bags, and announced five novices and two recalls as their replacements. On top of that, one of the openers will be subjected to a disciplinary investigation for allegedly faking an injury. As actions of the PCB administration go, this is unprecedented. As human behaviour goes, this is lunacy. These developments have unleashed a deafening outrage , triggering embarrassing news headlines and sarcastic social media memes. That Pakistan’s cricket establishment has degenerated into such farce should come as no surprise. The PCB chairman has always been a handpicked political appointee — merit be damned. And since a fish rots from the head, there you have it. Yes, sometimes you will get lucky with the arrival of a Nur Khan or an Arif Abbasi at the helm, but these are fortuitous exceptions. A national cricket board chief is meant to be an elected official, voted in by representatives of regional cricket associations. This makes the position approachable and accountable. Instead, the practice in Pakistan is for the prime minister to dole out the PCB chairmanship as a favour or reward to an ally or acolyte. The typical outcome is whimsical and incom­­petent governance. Over time, this has resulted in a cricketing infrastructure that lacks the ability to identify, nurture and promote the best talent available. As actions of the PCB administration go, this is unprecedented. As human behaviour goes, this is lunacy. The one silver lining in this whole fiasco is that the ire of the cricket-following public has finally been deflected away from the players and squarely onto the PCB and its leadership. This is as it should be. We would normally have the players in our gunsights, as they are the most visible and hence the most obvious targets. But the blame ultimately lies elsewhere. To shine on the international stage, a cricketing tradition must rest on three pillars — an avid fan base, a rich talent pool, and a capable administration. There’s no question about the avidity of the fan base, nor about the richness of the talent pool. Just look at the whiplash that Pakistan’s cricket supporters go through with every victory and every defeat; that tells you all you need to know about their passionate commitment. As for talent, a country that has managed to produce all-time legends such as Javed Miandad, Zaheer Abbas, Wasim Akram, Waqar Younis and Younis Khan (among many others), is certainly not lacking in cricketing ability. That leaves governance and management, by far the most compromised pillar in Pakistan’s cricket edifice. It is honestly very hard to fathom what deliberations would have taken place in the upper echelons of the PCB that led to such a ridiculous knee-jerk outcome. It couldn’t have come from the high-performance director Aqib Javed, the lone international cricketer in PCB’s C-suite, because he would surely know better. Quite possibly Aqib mi­­ght have advocated for a more measured appro­ach. Yes, he has been staunchly defending the PCB’s actions in the media and on public forums, but the PCB command structure leaves him little choice. In all likelihood, the decision-making came solely from the PCB chief, Mr Mohsin Naqvi, himself. He may have asked for input from other bigwigs in the PCB’s corporate hierarchy, but none of them have any serious cricketing credentials. One can easily imagine them trying to guess what the boss wanted to hear, and then echoing it implicitly and explicitly. What thought process did Mohsin Naqvi undertake to do what he did? By the looks of it, not a very rigorous one. He is, to begin with, an overburdened man, holding the portfolio of federal minister for interior and narcotics control, in addition to his PCB hat. Moreover, he has emerged as a key member of the diplomatic team seeking peace in the Middle East, having visited Iran no less than six times since hostilities started. This mandate amounts to averting ‘World War III’, no small assignment. So we can reasonably conclude that Mr Naqvi as a cricket administrator is at best distracted, and at worst negligent. Meanwhile, there is still the issue of the cricket itself. Pakistan are scattered and scarred after losing the first two Tests. One can only imagine the terrified mood in the camp as the team anticipates the third and final Test, starting in Birmingham on Sept 9. Cricket is a funny game and a turnaround in Pakistani fortunes is theoretically possible, but the odds are of course heavily against it. The team is weak and demoralised, if not outright traumatised. Cricket fans have been left wondering if this is the worst Pakistani cricket outfit ever. It is worth remembering, however, that Pakistan cricket has seen much worse, both on and off the field. In 2002, in what is easily our worst Test scorecard ever, Pakistan faced Australia in a Test in Sharjah, totaling 59 in the first innings and 53 in the second, losing (naturally) by an innings — even though that team had included some great names. Then, in 2009, there was the terrorist attack outside Lahore’s Gaddafi Stadium that nearly killed the visiting Sri Lankan side. And in 2010 we had the spot-fixing disaster, which ended two highly promising fast-bowling careers and sent three Pakistani cricketers to London’s Crown Court, and thence to prison. Thankfully, we are now far removed from those catastrophes. The challenge ahead is to improve on-field performance and restore our international competitiveness. It won’t happen overnight, but if we can somehow manage to sort out the Gordian knot that is the Pakistan Cricket Board, that would make for an appropriate start to a revival of lost glory. Security forces kill over 20 terrorists during multiple engagements in KP: ISPR. Security forces killed over 20 terrorists during multiple engagements in Khyber Pakhtunkhwa between September 3 and 5, the military’s media affairs wing said on Sunday. The ISPR statement mentioned an engagement in KP’s North Waziristan on the night between August 31 and September 1. Security forces had initially killed 15 terrorists who were trying to infiltrate into Pakistan through its border with Afghanistan at the time. Following that, 10 more terrorists holed up in the area were killed, the statement said, adding that a total of 25 terrorists trying to enter Pakistan had been killed in that event. In another encounter in North Waziristan, movement of another group of terrorists along the Pakistan-Afghanistan border was picked up by the security forces. “Own troops effectively engaged this group of khawarij . As a result of precise and skillful engagement, seven khawarij were neutralised,” the ISPR statement said. Separately, four more terrorists were killed in two different encounters in Kohat and Dera Ismail Khel during joint operations, according to ISPR. It said, “These repeated incidents along the Pakistan-Afghanistan border have once again vindicated Pakistan’s persistent stance regarding the abject failure of the Afghan Taliban regime to deny the use of Afghan soil to the terrorist organisation, under their patronage, for cross-border terrorism. “The Afghan Taliban regime has consistently failed to ensure effective border management and honour its international counter-terrorism obligations.” The statement added that security forces “remain resolute and unwavering in their commitment to defend the nation’s frontiers”. “Sanitization operations are being conducted to eliminate any other India-sponsored kharji found in the area as relentless counter-terrorism campaign under the vision ‘Azm-i-Istehkam’ (as approved by Federal Apex Committee on National Action Plan) by security forces and law enforcement agencies of Pakistan will continue at full pace to wipe out the menace of foreign-sponsored and -supported terrorism from the country,” the statement read.

Chad Blames Sudan’s Army for Strikes on Convoy cmoore Fri, 08/28/2026 - 12:46 Latest Updates Africa Asia-Pacific Europe Latin America & Caribbean Middle East & North Africa United States Global Issues & Institutions My Reading List Analyst's Notebook / Africa 28 August 2026 2 minutes Chad Blames Sudan’s Army for Strikes on Convoy Crisis Group expert Fulbert Ngodji sheds light on an air raid in Chad that is believed to have destroyed trucks carrying supplies for one of the main belligerents in the Sudanese civil war. Share BlueSky Email Facebook Linkedin Twitter Whatsapp Save Print Fulbert Ngodji Analyst, Central Africa https://www.linkedin.com/in/fulbert-dg-ngodji-459054147/ Related Tags Chad Sudan On 22 August, the Chadian army accused its Sudanese counterpart of attacking a convoy in eastern Chad. In a televised statement , the army spokesman said Sudanese army aircraft and drones had pursued the trucks over 100km into Chad two days earlier before striking them in Mourdi department, Ennedi-Est province. Pro-Sudanese army online platforms circulated images purporting to show the army disabling several vehicles carrying supplies for the Rapid Support Forces (RSF), the paramilitary group it has been fighting for control of Sudan since April 2023. The Sudanese army has not directly responded to the allegation, merely affirming its “respect for Chad’s sovereignty” in a 27 August statement . Open-source data and confidential sources have allowed Crisis Group to piece together a plausible account of what happened. A convoy of around 200 military pickup trucks reportedly left Libya and crossed Chad en route to Sudan. The Sudanese army or one of its allies then appears to have attacked the trucks near the Chadian border, as part of a months-long aerial campaign to disrupt RSF supply lines from Libya. About 70 vehicles tried to escape by crossing back into Chad, where they were destroyed. Satellite imagery showing smoke rising from the area seems to corroborate the Chadian army’s charge. It is unclear, however, who was driving the trucks and what they were carrying. The Chadian army did not address these questions. The conflict in Sudan has repeatedly spilled into Chad, primarily through an influx of refugees and, more recently, cross-border violence. Since December 2025, Chad’s eastern border has seen at least eleven incursions and drone strikes, which reportedly have killed about 30 civilians and soldiers. N’Djamena has typically sent military reinforcements or closed the border in response, but to this point it had refrained from blaming either of the main warring parties in Sudan. The 22 August statement is a departure from the previous caution, raising concerns that Chad will be drawn deeper into the civil war next door. Not only could Chad’s allegation sharpen tensions with the army-aligned authorities in Khartoum, but it could also reinforce perceptions that N’djamena has chosen sides in Sudan’s war, indirectly supporting the RSF. These perceptions are based on evidence that the United Arab Emirates has been using Chadian territory to provide the RSF with weapons and equipment. N’Djamena and Abu Dhabi have consistently denied these claims. Even so, escalation is unlikely: a confrontation would be costly for both N’Djamena and the Sudanese army. President Mahamat Déby is struggling to contain anger among his Zaghawa ethnic group, which has dominated Chad’s ruling elite since 1990. Many Zaghawa resent the government’s alleged backing of the RSF. The Sudanese army, meanwhile, controls Khartoum and much of central, northern and eastern Sudan, but remains locked in a war of attrition with no end in sight. Still, if the Sudanese army did in fact conduct the strike, its scale sets a dangerous precedent and could pave the way for more attacks by Sudanese belligerents, fuelling risks of a response by N’Djamena.
